meta.source: CASEL's SEL Framework (Collaborative for Academic, Social, and Emotional Learning), the "CASEL wheel," 2020 revision
meta.license_note: CASEL's SEL Framework (c) CASEL, all rights reserved; CASEL's own terms permit noncommercial use in preschool-through-high-school education, which is the only use made of it here. The five competency names and the official sub-competency names are CASEL's; every paraphrase here is written for this project, never CASEL's own text.
meta.scope_note: CASEL is a general social-and-emotional-learning framework, not a CS-specific one -- it's cataloged here as an orthogonal standard a lesson can also be checked against, alongside the CS/digital-literacy frameworks above. The sub-competency list below reflects CASEL's current (2020-revision) wheel, confirmed directly against casel.org on the extraction date; an earlier (January 2017) version of the wheel used a shorter, less equity-explicit list under each competency, so a secondary source describing CASEL's sub-competencies may not match this file if it's citing that older wheel.
meta.codes_note: Codes are this project's own sequential numbering, not CASEL's: <prefix>.<n> per competency, in the order CASEL's own wheel lists them within that competency (SA=Self-Awareness, SM=Self-Management, SOC=Social Awareness, REL=Relationship Skills, RDM=Responsible Decision-Making). CASEL does not number or code its sub-competencies itself, only names them, the same situation unesco-mil was in.
meta.settings_note: CASEL frames these five competencies as taught and reinforced across four coordinated settings, not in a classroom alone: classrooms, schools, homes, and communities.

groups.name: Self-Awareness
groups.paraphrase: Understanding your own emotions, values, and identity well enough to see how they shape your behavior, and seeing yourself accurately with a confident, growth-oriented outlook.

items.name: Integrating personal and social identities
items.paraphrase: A student's sense of self blends their personal identity with the social identities, family, culture, community, they're part of, not one or the other alone.

items.name: Identifying personal, cultural, and linguistic assets
items.paraphrase: Recognizing the strengths that come from a student's own background, culture, and language is part of self-awareness, not something separate from it.

items.name: Identifying one's emotions
items.paraphrase: Naming what you're actually feeling, accurately and specifically, is the starting point for managing it.

items.name: Demonstrating honesty and integrity
items.paraphrase: Being self-aware includes being honest with yourself and others about who you are and what you value.

items.name: Linking feelings, values, and thoughts
items.paraphrase: Noticing how an emotion, a belief, and a thought connect to each other is what makes self-awareness more than just naming a feeling in isolation.

items.name: Examining prejudices and biases
items.paraphrase: Looking honestly at your own prejudices and biases, rather than assuming you don't have any, is part of understanding how your thinking shapes your behavior.

items.name: Experiencing self-efficacy
items.paraphrase: Believing you're capable of doing something well is what lets a student actually attempt it.

items.name: Having a growth mindset
items.paraphrase: Treating ability as something that develops with effort, not a fixed trait, changes how a student responds to a setback.

items.name: Developing interests and a sense of purpose
items.paraphrase: Knowing what you care about and why gives direction to the choices you make.

groups.name: Self-Management
groups.paraphrase: Regulating your own emotions, thoughts, and behavior well enough to work toward a goal, even under stress.

items.name: Managing one's emotions
items.paraphrase: Regulating a strong emotion in the moment, rather than being controlled by it, is a learnable skill.

items.name: Identifying and using stress management strategies
items.paraphrase: Recognizing stress and having a real strategy for it, not just getting through it, is part of self-management.

items.name: Exhibiting self-discipline and self-motivation
items.paraphrase: Following through on something without someone else pushing you to is what separates self-management from just complying.

items.name: Setting personal and collective goals
items.paraphrase: Setting a goal for yourself and setting one for a group you're part of are related but separate skills, both part of self-management.

items.name: Using planning and organizational skills
items.paraphrase: Breaking a goal into steps and keeping track of them is what turns an intention into a finished result.

items.name: Showing the courage to take initiative
items.paraphrase: Starting something before being told to, even when the outcome is uncertain, takes a kind of courage that's part of self-management.

items.name: Demonstrating personal and collective agency
items.paraphrase: Believing your own actions, and your group's actions together, can actually change an outcome is what makes effort feel worthwhile.

groups.name: Social Awareness
groups.paraphrase: Understanding and empathizing with people whose backgrounds, cultures, and circumstances differ from your own, including the norms and systems that shape their situation.

items.name: Taking others' perspectives
items.paraphrase: Genuinely considering how a situation looks from someone else's point of view, not just assuming your own view is universal.

items.name: Recognizing strengths in others
items.paraphrase: Noticing what someone else is good at is part of social awareness, not just noticing their emotions.

items.name: Demonstrating empathy and compassion
items.paraphrase: Empathy is understanding what someone else feels; compassion is caring enough to want to help.

items.name: Showing concern for the feelings of others
items.paraphrase: Paying attention to how your words or actions land on someone else is a basic form of social awareness.

items.name: Understanding and expressing gratitude
items.paraphrase: Recognizing when someone has helped you, and saying so, is part of being socially aware, not just being polite.

items.name: Identifying diverse social norms, including unjust ones
items.paraphrase: Different settings have different unwritten rules for behavior, and some of those rules are themselves unfair, worth noticing rather than just following.

items.name: Recognizing situational demands and opportunities
items.paraphrase: Reading what a specific situation actually calls for, rather than applying one fixed script everywhere, is part of social awareness.

items.name: Understanding the influences of organizations and systems on behavior
items.paraphrase: People's behavior is shaped by the institutions and systems around them, not just by personal choice alone.

groups.name: Relationship Skills
groups.paraphrase: Building and keeping healthy relationships across a range of people and groups, through clear communication, cooperation, and constructive conflict.

items.name: Communicating effectively
items.paraphrase: Getting your actual meaning across, and listening well enough to receive someone else's, is the foundation every other relationship skill builds on.

items.name: Developing positive relationships
items.paraphrase: Building a relationship that's actually healthy takes deliberate effort, not just spending time near someone.

items.name: Demonstrating cultural competency
items.paraphrase: Working well across cultural differences means knowing enough to engage respectfully, not just being polite in the abstract.

items.name: Practicing teamwork and collaborative problem-solving
items.paraphrase: Solving a problem as a team is a different skill from solving the same problem alone, and it has to be practiced on its own.

items.name: Resolving conflicts constructively
items.paraphrase: Working through a disagreement so both sides actually come out better, instead of just ending the argument, is a specific skill.

items.name: Resisting negative social pressure
items.paraphrase: Saying no to pressure from a peer group takes a skill of its own, separate from knowing the right answer.

items.name: Showing leadership in groups
items.paraphrase: Leading a group well means helping it function better, not just being the one in charge.

items.name: Seeking or offering support and help when needed
items.paraphrase: Knowing when to ask for help, and when to offer it, is a relationship skill most people have to learn deliberately.

items.name: Standing up for the rights of others
items.paraphrase: Speaking up when someone else is being treated unfairly, even when it doesn't affect you directly, is part of maintaining a healthy relationship with a community.

groups.name: Responsible Decision-Making
groups.paraphrase: Making a thoughtful choice about your own behavior and social interactions by weighing evidence, ethics, safety, and the well-being of everyone affected.

items.name: Demonstrating curiosity and open-mindedness
items.paraphrase: Being willing to ask a real question and consider an answer you didn't expect is what makes a decision actually informed.

items.name: Learning how to make a reasoned judgment after analyzing information, data, and facts
items.paraphrase: Working from evidence to a conclusion, rather than from a gut reaction, is the core move of responsible decision-making.

items.name: Identifying solutions for personal and social problems
items.paraphrase: Generating real options for a problem, not just naming that a problem exists, is where responsible decision-making actually does its work.

items.name: Anticipating and evaluating the consequences of one's actions
items.paraphrase: Thinking ahead to what a choice will actually lead to, for yourself and for other people, before making it.

items.name: Recognizing how critical thinking skills are useful both inside and outside of school
items.paraphrase: Critical thinking taught in a classroom is meant to transfer to decisions made outside it, not stay confined to schoolwork.

items.name: Reflecting on one's role to promote personal, family, and community well-being
items.paraphrase: Looking back at how your own choices affected the people and communities around you, not just yourself, is part of making better ones next time.

items.name: Evaluating personal, interpersonal, community, and institutional impacts
items.paraphrase: A single decision can ripple out from an individual to a relationship to a whole community or institution, and responsible decision-making means weighing all of those levels, not just the nearest one.
